native_result.query: How does the median wealth of white individuals compare to that of black and Hispanic individuals from 1985 onwards?
native_result.HypoA: 1985 onwards, white individuals have a significantly higher median wealth compared to black and Hispanic individuals.
native_result.HypoB: С 1985 года медианное семейное чистое богатство у респондентов NON-BLACK NON-HISPANIC (трактованных как прокси white) стабильно выше, чем у BLACK и HISPANIC, и разрыв со временем растёт: в 1985 медианы $3,500 (white) vs $1,600 (black) vs $500 (Hispanic), к 1996 — $42,600 vs $9,800 vs $2,562.5. Отношение white/black выросло с 2.2x до 4.35x, white/Hispanic — с 7.0x до 16.6x. Hispanic-группа имеет наихудшую медиану во все годы и наибольшую долю нулевого wealth (~19–34%), black-группа растёт быстрее в абсолюте, но отстаёт в 2–4.7 раза. Вывод устойчив к attrition: на сбалансированной панели (n=5,739) те же выводы с ratios 2.4x–17.8x. Оговорки: значения номинальные; негативы — реальные долги, нули — реальный нулевой wealth (сохранены); выборка с неполным откликом — к 1996 остаётся ~56% исходной, группа white-прокси теряет 38% против ~20% у minority-групп, что может смещать медианы 1996 года, но чувствительность-проверка показывает, что направление вывода не меняется.

sub_hypo.text: Median family net wealth is consistently higher for NON-BLACK NON-HISPANIC respondents, treated as a white proxy, than for BLACK and HISPANIC respondents in 1985, 1990, and 1996, and the gaps increase over time. Medians rise from $3,500, $1,600, and $500 respectively in 1985 to $42,600, $9,800, and $2,562.5 in 1996. White/black ratios increase from 2.2 to 4.35, and white/Hispanic ratios from 7.0 to 16.6.
sub_hypo.context: NLSY79 respondents with nonmissing wealth in each analyzed year (1985, 1990, 1996). Wealth is nominal; negative values represent actual debts and zeros represent actual zero wealth, both retained.
sub_hypo.relations: White-proxy median wealth exceeds both minority-group medians in every analyzed year; absolute gaps and white/minority median ratios widen over time.

sub_hypo.text: HISPANIC respondents have the lowest median family net wealth in all analyzed years and the largest share of zero wealth, approximately 19–34%. BLACK respondents experience faster absolute wealth growth than HISPANIC respondents but have median wealth approximately 2–4.7 times below the white-proxy group.
sub_hypo.context: NLSY79 respondents with nonmissing wealth in 1985, 1990, or 1996, analyzed separately by year; nominal negative and zero wealth values are retained.
sub_hypo.relations: Hispanic median wealth is consistently lowest and its zero-wealth share highest; black median wealth grows faster in absolute terms than Hispanic median wealth but remains below white-proxy median wealth.

sub_hypo.text: The direction of the racial/ethnic wealth differences and their widening over time persists in a balanced panel of 5,739 respondents, with white/minority median wealth ratios ranging from 2.4 to 17.8.
sub_hypo.context: Sensitivity analysis restricted to NLSY79 respondents with nonmissing family net wealth in all three years: 1985, 1990, and 1996. Nominal values, including debts and zeros, are retained.
sub_hypo.relations: Restricting analysis to the balanced panel preserves the wealth ordering and widening disparities observed in the available-response sample.

sub_hypo.text: Wealth-response attrition differs by racial/ethnic group: retention from 1985 to 1996 is 80.5% for BLACK respondents, 80.3% for HISPANIC respondents, and 61.6% for the white-proxy group. By 1996, approximately 56% of the original sample remains. Greater white-proxy attrition may bias 1996 medians, although the balanced-panel sensitivity analysis preserves the direction of the conclusions.
sub_hypo.context: NLSY79 wealth-response availability, including group-specific retention from 1985 to 1996 and comparison with the original sample.
sub_hypo.relations: White-proxy respondents have lower retention and greater attrition than BLACK and HISPANIC respondents; potential attrition bias does not reverse the observed disparities in the balanced-panel check.
